newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Premium vintage seen for Australian wine in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Premium vintage seen for Australian wine in 1997.

text.p: The Australian wine industry is ripe for continued growth after new vineyard plantings and favourable late conditions produced a record premium crush.
However, overall grape tonnages and yields are down on 1996 and a shortfall in red wine supplies is set to continue.
Industry estimates for the nearly-ended 1997 vintage range from 770,000 to 830,000 tonnes, down on 1996's 885,000 tonne record, but still expected to be the second highest on record.
New plantings are expected to have made up for lower yields in the premium grapes which are pushing exports and margins.
"It is a record premium crush and the quality is outstanding, it was quite a remarkable vintage," Winemakers' Federation of Australia chief executive Ian Sutton told Reuters.
Sutton said continued growth and profitability was setting up the industry well as a medium/long-term investment prospect.
With about 20,000 hectares of premium varieties, mostly reds, planted in the last four years, the Federation sees grape output of 900,000 tonnes in 1998, rising to one million in 1999.
Australia's largest wine maker, Southcorp Holdings Ltd, said the 1997 vintage consolidated last year's record harvest and continued the trend to premium stocks.

However, Southcorp Wines' chief executive Bruce Kemp said the industry would have welcomed a bigger overall vintage, particularly more premium reds. "If we had got 20 percent more (red) grapes, we probably still would have said we did not have enough against the global demand for red wine," he said.
The industry estimates its shortfall of premium reds - fuelled by rising demand and a disastrous 1995 vintage - to continue at least another five years.
A heatwave in February raised fears of a sharply lower grape intake but an 'Indian summer' prolonged ripening and boosted the vintage, now emerging as the highest quality in many years.

The overall tonnage reduction in this year's vintage came mainly from lower intakes of the lower-grade commercial varieties, such as sultana - a cask wine staple - with crops affected by frost and generally lower demand.

The Federation estimates the 1997 intake of premium varieties at about 490,000 tonnes - up on last year's 477,000 but down on earlier expectations of around 515,000 - with the sultana intake down to about 100,000 tonnes from 190,000.

It said premium reds production was expected to be about the same as last year, with premium whites up by about five percent. Kemp said Southcorp's intake of commercial varieties was down on its 1996 crush of 180,000 tonnes but its premium supplies were about the same as last year.
With the shortfall in premium red supplies, Southcorp was reassessing its long term planting strategy. He said there could be further pressure this year on red wine prices.
BRL Hardy Ltd crushed about 135,000 tonnes this year, down on 1996's 147,500 tonnes, but with premium stocks up 20 percent, operations and technical manager Angus Kennedy said.
He said the company was well-placed to meet projections for double digit sales growth.
"We have had a tremendous first quarter and the supply is there from this vintage to enable that to continue so we are pretty chuffed at this stage," Kennedy said.
He said grape prices were generally up about five percent overall, with more pressure on red varieties.

Orlando Wyndham, owned by the French Pernod Ricard group and maker of Australia's most successful wine export brand, Jacob's Creek, said it had come close to its target intake of 105,000 tonnes, up overall on last year's 95,000 tonnes, and was impressed with quality.
"I cannot think of a year when we have had a higher percentage of red that good ... it was really an excellent vintage," chief winemaker Philip Laffer said.
He said Orlando's white wine export sales would be limited by low supplies until the 1997 vintage became available, and it was probably five years away from satisfying red wine demand.

"One of the problems is that no-one in Australia knows how really big this international market is, because while you have got markets on allocation (limited supplies) you are not going out trying to develop new markets because that just adds to the embarassment you have already got," he said.
"Who knows how much latent demand is sitting out there?" -- Sydney newsroom 651-2 9373-1800
